clinical_scope.population: Adults and young people aged 16 years or older unless otherwise specified by local protocol
clinical_scope.intended_use: High-risk candidate retrieval and guideline-based verification for suspected Sepsis.
clinical_scope.important_boundary: This graph supports clinical reasoning and missed-diagnosis risk reduction; it is not an autonomous diagnostic system.

aliases: Life-threatening organ dysfunction due to infection

distinctions.description: Septic shock is a subset of sepsis with circulatory and cellular/metabolic abnormalities associated with higher mortality; operationally it includes vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg and serum lactate greater than 2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitation.

basic_info.working_definition: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
why_high_risk_for_missed_diagnosis: Early findings are nonspecific and may mimic viral illness, dehydration, medication effects, cardiopulmonary disease, metabolic disorders, or postoperative states.
Fever may be absent, especially in older adults, immunocompromised patients, or patients using antipyretics or corticosteroids.
Hypotension may be late; normal blood pressure does not exclude early sepsis.

Organ dysfunction may present as confusion, tachypnea, hypoxemia, oliguria, thrombocytopenia, elevated creatinine, bilirubin elevation, or elevated lactate rather than obvious localizing infection symptoms.
Sepsis can progress rapidly to shock, tissue damage, organ failure, and death without fast recognition and treatment.
basic_info.time_sensitivity: Potentially life-threatening; suspected sepsis requires urgent recognition, infection source evaluation, organ dysfunction assessment, escalation when indicated, and guideline-based emergency management.

case_input_normalization.single_pass_missing_information_policy: Do not ask follow-up questions. Mark absent data as not_provided and explain how missing data limits verification.
case_input_normalization.normalization_patch_note: Normalization rules were systematized on 2026-06-28 to support retrieval from textual triggers, abbreviations, and numeric clinical facts. Rules map common case expressions to graph node ids where available. They are retrieval signals, not autonomous diagnostic criteria.

activation_logic.value: Retrieve the sepsis disease graph when a case contains suspected/confirmed infection OR possible infection source plus acute systemic deterioration, physiologic derangement, organ dysfunction, or high-risk host features.

guideline_verification_pathway.step_name: Establish whether infection is suspected or plausible
positive_criteria: Clinician or case text states infection is suspected or confirmed
Localizing infection symptoms or signs are present
Recent procedure/device/wound plus systemic deterioration
Imaging, culture, urinalysis, wound exam, CSF, respiratory findings, or abdominal findings suggest infection

guideline_verification_pathway.step_name: Assess acute physiologic derangement and screening signal
positive_criteria: Hypotension, MAP <65 mmHg, or marked blood pressure drop from baseline
Tachypnea or increased work of breathing
Hypoxemia or new oxygen requirement
Altered mental status
Fever or hypothermia
Tachycardia
Poor perfusion signs such as mottling, cool extremities, or delayed capillary refill

attributes.value: In acutely ill hospitalized adults, NEWS/NEWS2/MEWS/SIRS are preferred over qSOFA as a single sepsis screening tool. qSOFA features may still be useful as risk signals but should not be the sole screen.

guideline_verification_pathway.step_name: Assess acute organ dysfunction compatible with sepsis
positive_criteria: Acute SOFA increase >=2 if enough data are available
New altered mental status
Respiratory dysfunction or hypoxemia
Hypotension, vasopressor need, or shock physiology
Acute kidney injury or oliguria
Thrombocytopenia or coagulopathy
Hyperbilirubinemia or liver dysfunction
Elevated lactate or other hypoperfusion features
Vasopressor requirement to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg after adequate fluid resuscitation
Serum lactate >2 mmol/L after adequate fluid resuscitation
Persistent hypotension or hypoperfusion despite fluids

guideline_verification_pathway.step_name: Check required diagnostic actions and missing critical tests
positive_criteria: Blood cultures collected or planned as soon as possible, ideally before antibiotics if this does not delay therapy
Serum lactate measured
Source-specific microbiology and imaging considered based on suspected source
Organ dysfunction labs available or ordered

value: Shock: immediate antimicrobials, ideally within 1 hour of recognition.
Probable or definite sepsis without shock: immediate antimicrobials, ideally within 1 hour of recognition.
Possible sepsis without shock: rapid time-limited investigation; if concern persists, administer antimicrobials within 3 hours from first suspicion.

guideline_verification_pathway.step_name: Assess fluid resuscitation and perfusion monitoring

value: Begin treatment and resuscitation immediately for sepsis/septic shock.
For sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, consider at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in the first 3 hours with frequent reassessment and individualization.
Use dynamic measures and/or capillary refill as adjuncts for ongoing resuscitation; use serial lactate when lactate is elevated or septic shock is present.

positive_criteria: Abscess, obstructed infected system, perforation, ischemic/necrotic tissue, infected device, necrotizing soft tissue infection, intra-abdominal source, empyema, or other focus requiring drainage/removal/debridement/control

guideline_verification_pathway.step_name: Evaluate alternative diagnoses and avoid premature closure

differential_diagnosis.why_confusable: Hypotension, tachycardia, respiratory distress, and skin findings can mimic septic shock.

differential_diagnosis.disease_name: Cardiogenic shock or acute myocardial infarction
differential_diagnosis.why_confusable: Hypotension, tachypnea, altered mental status, elevated lactate, and pulmonary edema can overlap.
Tachycardia, hypotension, poor perfusion, altered mental status, and lactate elevation overlap.
features_supporting_index_disease: organ dysfunction disproportionate to volume loss

differential_diagnosis.why_confusable: Dyspnea, tachycardia, hypoxemia, hypotension, syncope, and lactate elevation can overlap.

differential_diagnosis.disease_name: Diabetic ketoacidosis or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
differential_diagnosis.why_confusable: Tachypnea, dehydration, altered mental status, acidosis, and infection trigger can overlap.
features_supporting_index_disease: infection source plus organ dysfunction; infection may precipitate DKA and both may coexist

differential_diagnosis.why_confusable: Shock, fever, weakness, abdominal pain, hyponatremia, and hypoglycemia can mimic sepsis.
May be a source/subtype of sepsis and also requires separate urgent disease-specific pathway.
features_supporting_index_disease: systemic infection signs plus organ dysfunction or shock

differential_diagnosis.why_confusable: Often causes sepsis; easily missed if skin findings are subtle early.
features_supporting_index_disease: organ dysfunction or shock due to infection; urgent source control needed

evidence_sources.title: The Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock (Sepsis-3)
evidence_sources.summary: Defines sepsis as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection and operationalizes organ dysfunction as an acute SOFA score increase of 2 or more.

evidence_sources.title: About Sepsis
evidence_sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
evidence_sources.summary: CDC describes sepsis as the body's extreme response to infection, a life-threatening emergency that can arise from gastrointestinal, lung, skin, or urinary tract infections and progress rapidly to tissue damage, organ failure, and death.

evidence_sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
evidence_sources.publisher: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
evidence_sources.summary: For acutely ill patients in hospital, recommends NEWS, NEWS2, MEWS, or SIRS over qSOFA as a single screening tool for sepsis.

evidence_sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
evidence_sources.publisher: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
evidence_sources.summary: States sepsis is a clinical diagnosis not ruled in or out by a single biomarker/test; recommends blood cultures as soon as possible, ideally before antimicrobials, and suggests measuring blood lactate.
evidence_sources.recommendation_strength: strong for blood cultures; conditional for lactate; good practice statement for biomarker limitation
evidence_sources.certainty: low for blood cultures and lactate

evidence_sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
evidence_sources.publisher: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
evidence_sources.summary: Recommends immediate antimicrobials, ideally within 1 hour for septic shock or probable/definite sepsis without shock; for possible sepsis without shock, recommends rapid investigation and antimicrobials within 3 hours if infection concern persists.
evidence_sources.recommendation_strength: strong for shock/probable-definite sepsis timing; conditional for possible sepsis without shock

evidence_sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
evidence_sources.publisher: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
evidence_sources.summary: Adults with sepsis or septic shock should be rapidly evaluated for anatomical diagnoses or infection sources requiring emergent source control; early source control is suggested ideally within 6 hours when required.

evidence_sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
evidence_sources.publisher: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
evidence_sources.summary: States sepsis and septic shock are medical emergencies requiring immediate treatment/resuscitation; suggests at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in the first 3 hours for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, with individualized reassessment.

evidence_sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
evidence_sources.publisher: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
evidence_sources.summary: Suggests serial lactate measurements to guide resuscitation in adults with sepsis and elevated lactate or septic shock.

evidence_sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
evidence_sources.publisher: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
evidence_sources.summary: Recommends norepinephrine as the first-line vasopressor for adults with septic shock.
evidence_sources.certainty: high vs dopamine; low vs epinephrine/selepressin

evidence_sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026
evidence_sources.publisher: Society of Critical Care Medicine / European Society of Intensive Care Medicine
evidence_sources.summary: Suggests measuring oxygenation by pulse oximeter or arterial blood gas with physical examination and clinical judgment.

evidence_sources.title: Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over: recognition, assessment and early management
evidence_sources.publisher: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
evidence_sources.summary: NICE guideline for people aged 16 or over who are not and have not recently been pregnant; covers recognition, early assessment, initial treatment, escalation, source finding/control, early monitoring, information/support, and training/education.

must_not: Do not state that sepsis is confirmed unless infection plus organ dysfunction criteria are satisfied by the case data or explicitly diagnosed by clinicians.
Do not rule out sepsis solely because fever, lactate elevation, leukocytosis, procalcitonin elevation, or positive cultures are absent.
Do not rely on qSOFA as the sole sepsis screening method.
Do not recommend a specific antibiotic regimen without local antimicrobial guidance, allergy history, infection source, renal/hepatic function, and resistance context.
Do not delay emergency escalation in the generated reasoning when shock, altered mental status, hypoxemia, or hypoperfusion is present.
Do not apply this adult graph to children, neonates, pregnant patients, or recently pregnant patients.
must_do: Always report missing critical information rather than asking follow-up questions.
Always separate supporting evidence, conflicting evidence, and missing evidence.
Always consider and report plausible noninfectious differentials when infection evidence is weak.
Always mark source control as a separate verification domain when an anatomical infectious source may require drainage, debridement, or device removal.
Always include a clinician-review safety note in final outputs.
